headline: Canada Sheds 84,000 Jobs as Tariff Fallout Batters Labour Market
executive_summary:
• Statistics Canada's February Labour Force Survey reported employment fell by 84,000 (-0.4%), pushing the unemployment rate up 0.2 percentage points to 6.7% and the employment rate down to 60.6%.6%, confirming a material loss of economic momentum as tariff-related uncertainty weighs on business investment and trade flows.2
  • Canada's merchandise trade deficit widened sharply in January to $3.6 billion from $1.3 billion in December, as exports fell 4.7% and imports declined 1.1%.0% in January, led by transportation equipment and machinery — sectors most exposed to cross-border supply chains and U.S. tariff measures.4
  • Industrial capacity utilization slipped to 78.5% in Q4 2025, down from a revised 78.9% in Q3, signalling growing slack in the production base.5
  • Ottawa and Ontario jointly announced funding to support tariff-impacted workers, while the federal government extended Work-Sharing temporary flexibilities to help employers avoid mass layoffs.6
  • Bill C-4, the Making Life More Affordable for Canadians Act, received Royal Assent on March 12, codifying affordability measures projected to save households hundreds of dollars annually.7
  • Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne requested a safeguard inquiry into imports of canned and frozen vegetables and prioritized an inquiry on wood products to prevent harmful trade diversion.8
  • Canada's software and computer services industries posted 8.5% revenue growth to $161.9 billion in 2024, providing a bright spot in the services economy.9
  • The federal government committed over $900 million to advance a Defence Industrial Strategy, aiming to bolster sovereignty-linked manufacturing and innovation capacity.10
  • A new Tripartite Advisory Council for Labour Policy was created to institutionalize worker and employer voices in an era of rapid trade disruption and economic restructuring.11
  • Canadian oilseed processors crushed a record 11.6 million tonnes of canola in 2025, up 1.6% year-over-year, benefiting from a record harvest and strong domestic processing demand.12

national.analysis:
The dominant macro narrative this week is unmistakable: Canada's labour market has buckled under the cumulative weight of tariff-driven uncertainty and a contracting goods-producing sector. Statistics Canada's February Labour Force Survey revealed employment fell by 84,000 (-0.4%), the employment rate slipped to 60.6%, and the unemployment rate rose 0.2 percentage points to 6.7%.6%, confirming that the economy has shifted from sluggish expansion to outright contraction.2 The confluence of a weakening labour market, shrinking output, and widening trade deficits presents Governor Tiff Macklem and the Bank of Canada with a challenging policy calculus at the current 2.25% policy rate.

The supporting data paint a picture of broad-based softening across the tradeable economy. Manufacturing sales declined 3.0% in January, with transportation equipment and machinery — both deeply integrated into Canada-U.S. supply chains — accounting for the bulk of the drop.4 The merchandise trade deficit ballooned to $3.6 billion in January from $1.3 billion in December, as exports fell 4.7% against a more modest 1.1% decline in imports.0%, dragged down by motor vehicle and parts sales as well as minerals and precious metals.13 Industrial capacity utilization eased to 78.5% in Q4 2025, down from a revised 78.9%, underscoring that businesses are pulling back on production rather than expanding into new capacity.5 At the industry level, management of companies (NAICS 55) contracted 2.1% month-over-month and 19.0% year-over-year, while mining and oil-and-gas extraction (NAICS 21) slipped 0.9% monthly despite Brent crude trading near US$99.56 per barrel.2

Not all sectors reflected this pattern of retreat. Building permits rose $607 million (+4.8%) to $13.3 billion in January, suggesting construction pipelines retain some forward momentum, consistent with the 0.3% monthly gain in construction industry GDP (NAICS 23).14 Utilities output surged 2.7% month-over-month, and Canada's software and computer services industries posted 8.5% revenue growth to $161.9 billion in 2024, highlighting the resilience of the knowledge economy.9 On the agricultural front, canola crushers processed a record 11.6 million tonnes in 2025, up 1.6% year-over-year, a welcome data point for Prairie producers navigating volatile commodity markets.12 The federal government also allocated up to $94.5 million over five years under the Sectoral Workforce Solutions Program across 14 organizations, and announced $24.7 million for apprenticeship training in Quebec alongside the provincial government.1516

Looking ahead, the risk profile tilts decidedly to the downside. Should U.S. tariffs remain at current levels or escalate, manufacturing and export sectors are likely to face further contraction, which would be expected to push unemployment materially above 7%. The federal-provincial partnership to support tariff-impacted workers in Ontario, and the extension of Work-Sharing flexibilities, suggest Ottawa is bracing for prolonged disruption rather than a short-lived shock.6 Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne's request for safeguard inquiries into canned and frozen vegetable imports, as well as wood products, signals concern that trade diversion could compound the damage from U.S. protectionism.8 If capacity utilization continues to slide below 78%, the output gap is likely to widen appreciably, adding to the case for further monetary easing — though the Bank of Canada must weigh this against energy-driven inflation pressures, with Brent crude hovering near the psychologically significant US$100 mark.

global.analysis: The U.S. economy remains the gravitational centre for Canadian trade outcomes, and the policy trajectory emanating from the Trump administration continues to inject profound uncertainty into cross-border commerce. With the Federal Reserve holding the federal funds rate at 4.25-4.50% and Chair Jerome Powell maintaining a cautious stance on further easing, the interest rate differential with Canada — whose policy rate sits at 2.25% — has widened to roughly 200 basis points. This gap is likely placing persistent downward pressure on the Canadian dollar, which in turn offers some offset for Canadian exporters competing on price but raises the cost of imported inputs and consumer goods.Canada's merchandise exports fell 4.7% in January, with the trade deficit widening to $3.6 billion — a deterioration strongly correlated with U.S. tariff measures and retaliatory uncertainty that has disrupted automotive, machinery, and lumber supply chains.2 The Governments of Canada and Ontario explicitly cited tariffs and global market shifts as the impetus for their joint worker-support announcement, underscoring that the bilateral trade friction is no longer an abstract risk but a materializing economic shock.S. trade policy under USTR Jamieson Greer and Secretary of Commerce Howard Lutnick will be the single most important external variable for Canada's near-term growth outlook. Finance Minister Champagne's safeguard inquiries into canned vegetables and wood products suggest Ottawa is preparing for trade diversion effects where goods originally destined for the U.S. market are rerouted into Canada at below-market prices, further pressuring domestic producers.4 Should the Fed begin easing later in 2026, narrowing the rate differential could stabilize the loonie, but it remains unclear how much influence monetary convergence can exert against a backdrop of structural trade barriers.

The trade diversion dynamics Ottawa is now actively monitoring — through safeguard inquiries on vegetables and wood products — are in part driven by the reconfiguration of global supply chains prompted by escalating U.S.-China tariffs under the Trump administration. As Chinese goods face higher barriers to the U.S. market, they are increasingly seeking alternative destinations, and Canada's open trade posture makes it a natural landing point for diverted flows.

For the second half of 2026, the trajectory of People's Bank of China monetary policy under Governor Pan Gongsheng will shape global commodity demand expectations. Should Beijing pursue more aggressive stimulus to counterbalance the drag from U.S. tariffs on Chinese exports, Canadian resource producers — particularly in energy, potash, and forestry — would be expected to benefit from firmer global pricing. However, the offsetting risk is that intensified Chinese stimulus leads to greater export volumes of manufactured goods that further depress prices in sectors where Canadian producers compete.

The United Kingdom remains a significant financial and trade counterpart for Canada, with the FTSE 100 closing at 10,261, up 20.1% year-over-year, suggesting that British firms have benefited from sterling weakness and global re-risking.2

The rate differential between the Bank of England under Governor Andrew Bailey and the Bank of Canada is a key transmission channel for bilateral capital flows. With the BoC at 2.25%, the spread against UK rates influences the CAD-GBP cross and the relative attractiveness of Canadian fixed-income assets to UK institutional investors. Canada's net foreign asset position declined by $110.0 billion to $1,801.1 billion at the end of Q4 2025, a shift that partly reflects valuation changes driven by currency movements and global portfolio rebalancing.The securities market data released by Statistics Canada showed Canadian governments and corporations borrowed a net $55.9 billion in debt securities in Q4, down from $88.5 billion the prior quarter, suggesting that financing conditions have tightened modestly.4 Should the UK pursue further bilateral trade liberalization with Canada, the financial services and technology corridors would be expected to see the most immediate benefit, given the demonstrated strength of Canada's $161.9-billion tech services sector.

provinces.name: Ontario
provinces.analysis:
Ontario's economy entered 2026 navigating the dual pressures of U.S. tariff uncertainty and a cooling domestic labour market, with the federal and provincial governments moving to cushion exposed workers. The governments of Canada and Ontario jointly announced funding to support workers impacted by tariffs and global market shifts as of March 10, 2026, signalling that trade-related displacement is already being felt in the province's industrial heartland.1

Transportation infrastructure activity is providing a modest offset to broader headwinds. Transport Canada announced on March 9, 2026 that a preclearance facility will open at Billy Bishop Toronto City Airport, a move that is likely to support cross-border business travel and improve the airport's competitive position relative to Pearson.2 Separately, Transport Canada committed up to $6.4 million to R.W. Tomlinson Ltd.'s Ontario Trap Rock facility for a Trap Rock Electrification project on March 13, 2026, targeting green shipping corridors that reduce input costs for construction material supply chains.3

On the policy front, the federal government's extension of Work-Sharing temporary flexibilities, announced March 11, 2026, is directly relevant to Ontario's manufacturing base, allowing employers facing demand shortfalls to reduce hours rather than execute mass layoffs.4 The creation of a new Tripartite Advisory Council for Labour Policy, announced March 12, 2026, suggests the federal government is institutionalizing labour-management dialogue in anticipation of a prolonged period of structural adjustment driven by trade realignment.5

Looking ahead, Ontario's near-term growth trajectory is likely to remain below potential should U.S. tariffs on Canadian goods persist at current levels. The Canada-Ontario worker support partnership and the Work-Sharing extensions provide a partial buffer, but would not be expected to fully offset the drag on manufacturing output and business investment. Infrastructure spending in green shipping and airport preclearance provides a modest positive impulse, though the scale of these investments is insufficient on its own to shift the provincial growth trajectory materially upward through mid-2026.

The federal government's restoration of Quebec's distinct role within the immigration system, formalized through a Canada-Quebec collaboration announcement on March 13, 2026, has direct implications for the province's skilled-trades pipeline.2 Quebec's construction and manufacturing sectors have persistently flagged skilled labour shortages, and the targeted immigration measure is designed to address those gaps while respecting the constitutional division of immigration responsibilities. This policy adjustment is likely to support near-term labour supply in sectors most exposed to tariff-driven demand shifts.

On the fiscal and labour policy front, the federal Work-Sharing flexibility extensions announced March 11, 2026 apply across Canada, including Quebec's aerospace and aluminum manufacturing clusters, which are among the most exposed to U.S. trade measures.3 The new Tripartite Advisory Council for Labour Policy, announced March 12, 2026, would be expected to incorporate Quebec's distinct labour relations framework given the province's historically active role in national labour consultations.4

Looking ahead, Quebec's near-term growth outlook hinges critically on the trajectory of U.S. tariffs targeting aluminum and aerospace inputs. Should current tariff levels persist through mid-2026, export-oriented manufacturers would be expected to curtail capital spending, partially offsetting gains from the province's ongoing public infrastructure cycle. The immigration policy recalibration announced in March 2026 provides a modest structural positive by easing worker shortages, but its impact on GDP growth is likely to materialize over a medium-term horizon rather than providing immediate cyclical support.

Alberta's economy in the opening months of 2026 is being shaped primarily by the intersection of oil price volatility, U.S. tariff threats on Canadian energy exports, and the federal government's active positioning of Canada as a pillar of IEA energy supply stability. Natural Resources Canada's March 13, 2026 statement affirmed Canada's status as the world's fourth-largest oil supplier and the largest within the IEA membership, a designation that directly reflects Alberta's production dominance.1 This framing has strategic implications for Alberta's investment climate as producers assess the durability of export access.

Energy sector confidence is also being shaped by the federal government's March 11, 2026 statement in support of strengthening global energy stability, which signals Ottawa's intent to leverage Canada's oil export capacity in international energy diplomacy.2 For Alberta's upstream sector, this federal posture is a modest positive, as it reduces the near-term risk of supply-constraining federal energy policy pivots. However, the IEA coordination also implies potential commitments to emergency stock releases or production coordination that could weigh on spot pricing.

Infrastructure investment in Calgary is providing a secondary economic impulse. The federal government announced a $4.4 million investment in a new Calgary Japanese Community Association community centre on March 14, 2026, funded through Infrastructure Canada's Green and Inclusive Community Buildings program.3 While modest in scale, this reflects the ongoing federal capital deployment in the Calgary CMA, and federal media advisories suggest further infrastructure announcements in Calgary were in progress as of the week of March 13, 2026.4

Looking ahead, Alberta's growth outlook for 2026 is likely to remain above the national average provided oil prices hold in a range that sustains breakeven economics for oil sands operators. Should U.S. tariffs on Canadian energy be extended or deepened, pipeline-dependent export volumes could face margin compression, dampening royalty revenues and provincial fiscal capacity. The federal government's IEA-aligned energy diplomacy is likely to provide a supportive backdrop for market diversification efforts, though new export corridor capacity would not be expected to come online within the current forecast horizon.

Looking ahead, Saskatchewan's growth trajectory for 2026 is likely to be shaped more by commodity price dynamics and export access than by domestic demand factors. New Brunswick's economy in early 2026 is contending with the intersection of U.S. tariff pressures on its forestry and energy sectors and an ongoing demographic transition that has seen notable population gains from international immigration over the prior two years. The federal government's Work-Sharing flexibility extensions announced March 11, 2026 are particularly germane to New Brunswick's sawmill and wood products manufacturing base, which operates within tight margins and would face significant layoff pressure if U.S. housing demand softens in response to tariff-driven cost increases.1

Labour market support mechanisms are being actively deployed. The rural TFW program adjustments announced March 13, 2026 have direct applicability to New Brunswick's blueberry, potato, and food processing sectors, all of which depend heavily on seasonal foreign workers given the province's limited domestic labour pool in rural communities.2 Premier Susan Holt's government has been actively promoting immigration as a structural solution to the province's demographic challenges, and the federal program adjustments announced in March 2026 align with those provincial priorities.

The new Tripartite Advisory Council for Labour Policy announced March 12, 2026 represents a potential channel through which New Brunswick's forestry and fisheries employers can elevate labour market concerns to the federal level, particularly regarding workforce training and adjustment programs that will be needed if tariff-related restructuring accelerates.3 New Brunswick's bilingual workforce profile also positions the province to benefit from Quebec-targeted immigration measures that may generate cross-provincial labour mobility as francophone workers seek employment opportunities.

Looking ahead, New Brunswick's near-term economic performance is likely to be below the national average growth rate, reflecting structural vulnerabilities in its trade-exposed resource sectors. However, the province's energy infrastructure, including the Point Lepreau nuclear generating station and LNG-adjacent coastal assets, provides a stable base of capital-intensive activity that is insulated from short-term tariff disruptions. Should the federal government accelerate energy infrastructure permitting as part of its IEA supply commitment strategy, New Brunswick's coastal export infrastructure could see renewed project interest over the medium term.

provinces.name: Newfoundland & Labrador
provinces.analysis:
Newfoundland and Labrador's economy in early 2026 is being driven primarily by offshore oil production at Hibernia, Terra Nova, and White Rose, with the federal government's IEA energy positioning providing a supportive policy backdrop for sustained offshore investment. Natural Resources Canada's March 13, 2026 statement confirming Canada's status as the world's fourth-largest oil producer and the largest within the IEA directly encompasses Newfoundland's Atlantic offshore output, which has been a growth driver as redevelopment projects extend field life.1 This federal framing reduces near-term regulatory risk for Atlantic offshore operators assessing future capital commitments.

The broader energy stability mandate articulated in Natural Resources Canada's March 11, 2026 statement creates a policy environment in which Newfoundland's offshore oil sector is positioned as a strategic national asset rather than a transition liability.2 This distinction matters for provincial fiscal planning, as royalty revenue projections are sensitive to both production volumes and the perceived long-term policy risk premium embedded in operator discount rates. A more stable federal energy policy posture is likely to support capital allocation decisions by offshore operators through the current planning cycle.

Labour market conditions in the province remain structurally challenged by outmigration and an aging workforce, and the federal Work-Sharing extensions announced March 11, 2026 provide a partial buffer for the province's manufacturing and processing employers operating under tariff uncertainty.3 However, the province's relatively small non-resource private sector limits the aggregate impact of these labour market interventions compared to larger industrial provinces.

Looking ahead, Newfoundland and Labrador's fiscal trajectory for 2026 is likely to hinge on oil price levels and production volumes from Atlantic offshore fields. Should Brent crude prices remain above the provincial budget's planning assumption, royalty revenues would be expected to provide a cushion against any softening in the provincial labour market or public sector wage pressures. The federal government's active IEA energy diplomacy is a meaningful supportive factor for the province's long-term investment climate, but near-term GDP growth will remain tightly correlated with offshore production rates.

provinces.name: Prince Edward Island
provinces.analysis:
Prince Edward Island's small and open economy in early 2026 is navigating a period of heightened trade uncertainty, with its agri-food export base — anchored in potato, seafood, and processed food products — facing potential exposure to U.S. tariff measures. The federal government's rural TFW program adjustments announced March 13, 2026 are directly relevant to P.E.I.'s seasonal agricultural and food processing labour market, where employer access to temporary foreign workers is a structural necessity given the island's limited resident labour pool.1

The Work-Sharing flexibility extensions announced March 11, 2026 provide a labour market safety net for P.E.I.'s manufacturing and processing employers should tariff-driven demand reductions materialize in the current year.2 While P.E.I.'s economy is too small to be significantly moved by any single federal program intervention, the cumulative effect of Work-Sharing, TFW access improvements, and labour policy council engagement represents a meaningful support package for the province's private sector employers operating under elevated uncertainty.

Tourism, which is a significant contributor to P.E.I.'s service sector, is likely to be influenced by the broader Canada-U.S. bilateral relationship. Any cooling in cross-border tourist flows driven by tariff-related diplomatic friction would be expected to weigh on the province's summer season hospitality sector, partially offsetting any gains from domestic Canadian tourism rerouting from U.S. destinations. The net effect on provincial GDP would depend on the relative magnitudes of these offsetting forces.

Looking ahead, P.E.I.'s economic outlook for 2026 is likely to remain close to trend growth, supported by ongoing public infrastructure investment, a stable agri-food export base, and population growth that has been among the strongest in the country on a percentage basis over the prior three years. The key downside risk remains trade policy escalation targeting agricultural goods, which would disproportionately affect P.E.I. relative to its provincial GDP weight given the island's structural dependence on agri-food export revenues.

provinces.name: Yukon
provinces.analysis:
Yukon's economy in early 2026 is characterized by a small and resource-dependent structure, with mining activity serving as the primary private sector engine alongside government services and tourism. The federal government's IEA energy supply commitments articulated in Natural Resources Canada's March 13, 2026 statement have indirect relevance to Yukon's critical minerals sector, as the broader federal posture of maximizing Canadian resource output creates a permissive policy environment for new mine development and exploration activity.1

Labour market conditions in Yukon are structurally tight, reflecting the territory's small resident workforce and geographic isolation. The federal government's rural TFW program adjustments announced March 13, 2026 are applicable to Yukon employers in resource extraction and hospitality, where domestic labour shortages are chronic.2 The Tripartite Advisory Council for Labour Policy announced March 12, 2026 may provide a forum for northern territories to raise their distinct labour market challenges, though the council's geographic reach and mandate will determine the extent to which Yukon's specific circumstances are addressed.3

Federal capital transfers remain essential to Yukon's public infrastructure development, and the Infrastructure Canada announcement activity observed in the week of March 13, 2026 — including the Iqaluit announcement and Calgary community infrastructure — suggests the federal infrastructure program pipeline continues to flow, with northern territories historically accessing this spending through distinct northern infrastructure streams.4 The Government of Yukon under Premier Ranj Pillai is likely to be actively engaging federal counterparts on capital project approvals given the territory's infrastructure deficit relative to southern provinces.

Looking ahead, Yukon's near-term economic outlook is likely to be supported by continued federal transfer dependency and a gradual recovery in mining sector investment if global critical mineral prices stabilize. The territory's growth trajectory remains highly sensitive to individual large project decisions — particularly in base metals and critical minerals — that can shift territorial GDP by meaningful percentages given the small economic base. Should U.S. critical mineral demand strengthen as supply chain diversification accelerates, Yukon's exploration sector would be expected to benefit disproportionately.

provinces.name: Northwest Territories
provinces.analysis:
The Northwest Territories' economy in early 2026 continues to be shaped by the diamond mining sector's secular decline — with the closure of major Diavik and Ekati operations representing a structural headwind — alongside emerging opportunities in critical minerals and territorial government-led infrastructure investment. The federal government's energy supply and IEA commitment statements issued by Natural Resources Canada on March 13, 2026 signal a broader federal posture of maximizing Canadian resource output, which is likely to extend to N.W.T.'s mineral and hydrocarbon resource base over the medium term.1

Labour market conditions in the N.W.T. under Premier R.J. Simpson's territorial government are constrained by the small resident population and the high cost of living in Yellowknife and remote communities. The federal TFW program adjustments announced March 13, 2026 are applicable to N.W.T. employers in mining, construction, and hospitality, where worker recruitment from southern Canada is expensive and often insufficient to meet operational requirements.2 The Work-Sharing flexibility extensions announced March 11, 2026 provide a partial buffer for territorial employers facing demand uncertainty, though the N.W.T.'s resource-extraction orientation means these provisions are more relevant to processing and support industries than to primary extraction operations.3

Infrastructure Canada's active announcement cycle in the week of March 13, 2026 — including a specific media advisory for an Iqaluit announcement involving Minister of Housing and Infrastructure Gregor Robertson — suggests the federal government's northern infrastructure spending pipeline remains active.4 The N.W.T. is likely to access comparable federal capital transfers through northern-specific infrastructure streams, supporting territorial roads, energy systems, and housing.

Looking ahead, the N.W.T.'s economic outlook for 2026 is likely to be below the national average growth rate given the structural adjustment in the diamond sector, though any new critical mineral development — particularly rare earths or lithium — could provide an upside scenario. Federal infrastructure spending and government services will remain the primary stabilizers of territorial economic activity, with the private sector recovering only gradually as mining investment pipelines mature through feasibility and permitting stages.

provinces.name: Nunavut
provinces.analysis:
Nunavut's economy in early 2026 operates under the most acute structural constraints of any Canadian jurisdiction, with high costs of living, significant infrastructure deficits, and an economy heavily dependent on federal transfers and a limited mining sector. The Infrastructure Canada media advisory for an announcement in Iqaluit on March 13, 2026, involving Minister of Housing and Infrastructure Gregor Robertson alongside other federal officials, signals direct federal capital deployment in the territory's capital.1 Given Nunavut's chronic housing shortage and inadequate community infrastructure, federal investment announcements of this nature carry disproportionate economic significance relative to their dollar value.

Under Premier P.J. Akeeagok, the Government of Nunavut has consistently prioritized housing supply and community infrastructure as the primary economic and social policy challenges facing the territory. The federal green and inclusive community buildings program — through which the $4.4 million Calgary Japanese community centre was funded on March 14, 2026 — represents a program stream potentially applicable to Nunavut community facility needs, though northern construction cost multipliers typically require adjusted funding envelopes for equivalent project scope.2

Labour market conditions in Nunavut are structurally distinct from those in provincial economies. The federal TFW program adjustments announced March 13, 2026 have limited direct applicability to Nunavut's economy given the territory's unique Inuit employment obligations under the Nunavut Agreement and the importance of Inuit Qaujimajatuqangit principles in workforce development policy.3 The Tripartite Advisory Council for Labour Policy announced March 12, 2026 would need to incorporate northern and Indigenous labour market perspectives to be meaningfully relevant to Nunavut's distinct employment landscape.4

Looking ahead, Nunavut's economic activity in 2026 is likely to be driven primarily by public sector construction, federal transfer spending, and any advancement of the Baffinland Mary River iron ore project or other mining sector developments. Should federal infrastructure commitments translate into shovel-ready housing and community projects following the March 2026 Iqaluit announcement, a modest positive impulse to territorial construction activity would be expected in the second half of 2026, subject to the logistics constraints that make northern construction inherently seasonal and cost-intensive.
